ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The figure shows a common-emitter BJT amplifier circuit. The input Vs is connected to the base node through a coupling capacitor; the base node is also connected to the upper and lower two 10 kΩ bias resistors, the upper one to VCC and the lower one to ground. The transistor is labeled β=50. The emitter is connected to ground through 1 kΩ, and has a bypass capacitor connected in parallel to ground. The collector is connected to VCC through RC, and the output is taken out through a coupling capacitor. Reasoning: According to AC small-signal analysis, the input coupling capacitor and emitter bypass capacitor are regarded as short circuits, and VCC is AC ground. Therefore the emitter is AC ground, and the resistance looking into the transistor from the base is rπ = β/gm = 50/(10 mS) = 50/0.01 S = 5000 Ω = 5 kΩ. The two 10 kΩ bias resistors are both connected from the base node to ground under AC, and their parallel value is 10 kΩ || 10 kΩ = 5 kΩ. So the input resistance RIN = rπ || 5 kΩ = 5 kΩ || 5 kΩ = 2.5 kΩ.

method.method_draft: Convert the circuit to its AC small-signal model: short the input coupling and emitter bypass capacitors, and ground VCC. The emitter is at AC ground because of the bypass capacitor, so the transistor contributes rπ = β/gm = 50/(10 mS) = 5 kΩ from base to ground. The two 10 kΩ bias resistors are also from the input/base node to AC ground, giving 10 kΩ || 10 kΩ = 5 kΩ. Therefore RIN = 5 kΩ || 5 kΩ = 2.5 kΩ.

method.method_draft: Place a test voltage vx at the input/base node. The upper and lower 10 kΩ resistors each draw vx/10 kΩ because VCC is AC ground. The transistor base path draws vx/rπ, where rπ = β/gm = 50/(10 mS) = 5 kΩ since the emitter is bypassed to AC ground. Thus ix = vx/10 kΩ + vx/10 kΩ + vx/5 kΩ.
